name: Kutchin
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Scollon, Ronald. 1975. A sketch of Kutchin phonology. University of Hawaii Working Papers in Linguistics 7(3): 17-87 (ERIC ED140605; archive.org).
catalog_locator: Sec. III.12 'Tone', p. 51 (ERIC internal p. 35; PDF leaf 36 of 72), continuing pp. 52-53 (leaves 37-38). of leaves 36-38 read.
catalog_quote: Kutchin has two tones, high and low. The high tone is a high falling pitch with a quick diminuition of intensity. ... Low tone is not marked since whatever is not high tone is low. ... In the prefix syllables tones are somewhat more difficult to determine because of two processes. Prefix high and low tone are not as high or low, respectively, as in the stem syllables. In addition, in casual speech stress is given to the penultimate syllable. This results in high tone in this position remaining high but preceding high tones being depressed. A low tone receiving stress is raised but not as high as the level of a high tone. These effects can be summarized by saying that in casual speech the last underlying high tone in a word will be high with the preceding high tones lowered. ... [p. 53] The explanation that seems most plausible to me is that FTYK is in the process of replacing tone with stress. All of the changes mentioned here result in the penultimate syllable receiving a higher pitch than the final syllable. It is only in the cases where underlying high tone is still marked that a final syllable receives high pitch and in the other cases no underlying pitch is represented. ... Of course, this is not the final word on tone and stress in Kutchin.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Gwich'in (gwic1235) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Leer 1976 'Spirantization and the Development of Suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan', was located and downloaded as an open ANLA scan (CA965L1976b; 86 leaves, no text, pp. 1-6 scanned): it is a comparative tonogenesis paper (PA constriction > stem tone), not about word stress, so no acquisition priority. The best first-hand stress statement found and read is Scollon 1975, 'A sketch of Kutchin phonology' (open at archive.org micro_IA41153432_0788), §III.12 Tone, pp. 51 and 53: Kutchin has two tones (high/low); 'in casual speech stress is given to the penultimate syllable', raising a low and depressing earlier highs, and Fort Yukon Kutchin 'is in the process of replacing tone with stress' — tentative by the author's own statement. Also downloaded from ANLA/YNLC and read: Ritter 1976 Fort McPherson noun dictionary (the phonological introduction previously flagged as unreachable — it is an orthography guide with no stress or tone statement), Ritter & Garnett 1990 'Aspects of Tone in Gwich'in' (tone exercises, no stress), Ritter 1974 dialect handout (segmental), YNLC 2003 Listening Exercises vol. 2 and YNLC alphabet (tone marking only, no stress).org and YNLC downloads.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Gwich'in (Kutchin) is a two-tone language (high vs. low, with a length correlate). Superimposed on tone, in casual speech, stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; a stressed high stays high while earlier highs are depressed, and a stressed low is raised (but not to high level). Scollon adds (p. 53) that Fort Yukon Kutchin appears to be replacing tone with (penultimate) stress, so that the penult is pitched higher than the final syllable except where an underlying final high tone is retained.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is described only for casual (rapid) speech; in slow, syllable-by-syllable speech the underlying tones surface (ex. 64). Final syllables may still carry an underlying high tone (e.g. gwitts'ik 'I am hurt', AVK and FTYK). The author calls this 'not the final word on tone and stress in Kutchin', expects penultimate stress to fall on stems followed by suffixes (raising a low stem), but lacks the data to check (p. 53). Question intonation makes the last syllable of a sentence high level, neutralizing tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (polysyllabic verb words with prefixes, e.g. k'enehiłdík 'I will return tomorrow'); observed in connected/casual speech vs. slow citation-style speech. Tone, not stress, is the primary lexical contrast; stress is a superimposed casual-speech prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Scollon 1975 describes Arctic Village Kutchin (AVK = Chandalar / Neets'aii Gwich'in, Alaska; fieldwork summer 1972) with comparison to Fort Yukon Kutchin (FTYK); both are Alaskan (western) Gwich'in dialects under gwic1235. He reports the penultimate-stress effect for AVK casual speech and argues FTYK is 'in the process of replacing tone with stress'. Canadian (Teetl'it / Gwichyah / Vuntut) varieties are not covered by this statement; I could not verify whether Glottolog assigns separate dialect glottocodes.

tone_statements.citation: Leer, Jeff (09//1990). Tone in Alaskan Gwich'
tone_statements.quote: Gwich'in (Kutchin, Dinjii Zhuh) is a low-marked tone language. This means that the vowel or vowels of a syllable may be marked for low tone (e.g. à, àa) or unmarked (e.g. a, aa). These are the simple tones. In Alaskan Gwich'in, what were originally two syllables may contract into a single syllable. If the tones of the original syllables are the same, the contracted syllable has that same tone; but if the tones of the original syllables are different, each tone is retained, giving rise to compound tones, namely either unmarked+low-marked (e.g. âa) or low-marked+unmarked (e.g. ãa).
tone_statements.locator: p. 1, opening paragraph; compound tones restated sec. 1.2, p. 6
tone_statements.summary: Two simple tones (low-marked vs unmarked) on each syllable; falling and rising 'compound tones' = two simple tones in one contracted syllable. Downdrift (1.3) called a natural tendency; sentence-final verb low-marking and a yes/no 'supertone' (sec. 2). Minimal pair, frame tests. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Yukon Native Language Centre (2003). Gwich'in Listening Exercises, Teetl'it Gwich'in dialect, vol. 2 (Section 3: Tones). Whitehorse: YNLC.
sources.quote: Gwich'in is a tonal language. This means that in certain words, some syllables always sound lower than the surrounding syllables. Because there are many more syllables that sound high than syllables that sound low, we just write low in Gwich'in by putting an acute accent ( ' ) on a low tone vowel. [...] The normal position for the main verb is at the end of the sentence. In this position, in declarative sentences, the last syllable will sound low.
sources.locator: 'Introduction to the Tone Listening Exercises', pp. 216-217
sources.note: Describes Teetl'it Gwich'in as a tone language (marked low vs unmarked high), tone perceived only relative to neighbouring syllables, possessed-noun tone alternations, sentence-final verb low. No mention of stress anywhere in the 207-page text (a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence: none).

sources.citation: Leer, Jeff (1976). Spirantization and the Development of Suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan. Ms. dated 7-21-76, 24 pp. + typescript 30 pp. ANLA CA965L1976b.
sources.quote: One of the major purposes of this paper is to formulate a hypothesis of the development of tone in modern Athabaskan from an earlier (pre-Proto-Athabaskan) system of vowel nuclei ... In the case of Athabaskan, however, the development of tone depended not only on the vowel nucleus, but on the final consonant of the syllable. If the final consonant was glottalized, the reflex of the tone is opposite of what it is if the final consonant was not glottalized.

tone.quote: Gwich'in (Kutchin, Dinjii Zhuh) is a low-marked tone language. This means that the vowel or vowels of a syllable may be marked for low tone (e.g. à, àa) or unmarked (e.g. a, aa). These are the simple tones. In Alaskan Gwich'in, what were originally two syllables may contract into a single syllable. If the tones of the original syllables are the same, the contracted syllable has that same tone; but if the tones of the original syllables are different, each tone is retained, giving rise to compound tones, namely either unmarked+low-marked (e.g. âa) or low-marked+unmarked (e.g. ãa).
tone.locator: p. 1, opening paragraph; compound tones restated sec. 1.2, p. 6
tone.summary: Two simple tones (low-marked vs unmarked) on each syllable; falling and rising 'compound tones' = two simple tones in one contracted syllable. Downdrift (1.3) called a natural tendency; sentence-final verb low-marking and a yes/no 'supertone' (sec. 2). Minimal pair, frame tests. Nothing on stress.
